notes.meaning: Job compares human life on earth to hard forced labor or military service. Just as a day-laborer has a set time of difficult work, every person has a limited time appointed by God on this earth. Job uses this to explain why he is so weary and why he yearns for his painful service to end.

A field laborer looks eagerly for the evening shadows so he can rest from the heat and receive his daily pay. In the same way, Job feels his long day of toil is finished, and he longs for the relief that rest brings. He believes his desire for relief in death is just as natural as a tired servant wanting the sunset.

Instead of receiving wages and rest, Job has been given months of empty sorrow and sleepless nights. His troubles have dragged on for a long time, bringing only disappointment. Even so, he recognizes that these painful months were appointed to him by God for some higher purpose.

Nighttime usually brings healing sleep, but for Job it brings only endless tossing and turning. As soon as he lies down, he dreads the dark hours and wonders when morning will finally come. His severe physical pain and distress of mind make it impossible for him to find any comfortable posture.

Job describes the horrible physical reality of his illness. Open sores cover his body, breeding worms, while dry scabs and dirt form crusts over his skin. Just when a sore seems to close, it breaks open and festers again, showing how fragile human bodies truly are.

Job compares the speed of his life to a weaver's shuttle moving back and forth across a loom. Though his nights feel terribly slow, his whole life seems to be running out fast without any thread of hope left for recovery on earth. Our days quickly slip away, which reminds us to use our fleeting time to serve the Lord.

Job turns from speaking to his friends and begins to pray directly to God. He asks the Lord to remember that human life is as frail and fleeting as a single breath of wind. From his point of view, his earthly joy is gone, and he will never see happy days in this world again.

Those who look at Job now will soon look in vain, because death will take him out of their sight. Even if God looks down upon him, Job will be gone from the earth in an instant, like someone who disappears under God's frown. God has the power to end mortal life with a single glance.

A cloud breaks apart in the sky, vanishes into thin air, and never gathers back together. In the same way, someone who dies and goes down to the realm of the dead does not return to this earthly life. Job is speaking about the present world, where physical life ends and cannot be lived over again.

When a person dies, he never comes back to live in his former house or carry on his earthly routines. Other people move in and take his place, and the home no longer knows him. Since this world will quickly forget us, we ought to seek an eternal home with God.

Because his life is almost over and cannot be lived again, Job refuses to keep quiet about his pain. He decides to pour out all the deep sorrow and anguish overflowing in his heart. While believers may honestly bring their grief to God, we should guard our speech so we do not speak rashly in anger.

Job asks God whether he is a wild sea or a fierce sea beast that needs to be chained and guarded with severe troubles. In ancient poetry, the stormy ocean was held back by God so it would not overwhelm the dry land. Job feels crushed and trapped, as if God treats him like a dangerous threat rather than a weak, suffering man.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that ancient Near Eastern poetry viewed the sea and deep-sea monsters as forces of chaos, and Job is asking why God treats a frail mortal as if he were one of those cosmic enemies.

notes.meaning: Job hopes to find relief from his pain when he lies down to rest at night. Instead of soothing him, his bed becomes a place of terror because frightening dreams and visions torment his mind as soon as he falls asleep. While his fever and illness contributed to these nightmares, Satan was also permitted to disturb his rest and shake his peace.

The agony of these nights is so intense that Job prefers choking or any quick death to living in his broken body. His frame is reduced to a miserable skeleton, and he feels he can bear the physical and mental torment no longer. Although his suffering was immense, wishing for death showed human weakness rather than patient trust in God's timing.

Job hates his present existence and declares that he has no desire to live forever in a broken, painful world. He asks God to withdraw His heavy hand and give him some relief during the few frail days he has left. Even when life seems completely empty, our days remain in God's hands.

Job asks why the Almighty God pays so much attention to a frail, lowly creature like man. This language echoes Psalm 8, but while the psalmist praises God for honoring man, Job wonders in his pain why God bothers to examine and trouble such a weak being. He feels unworthy of such intense divine focus.

Job complains that God visits him every single morning with fresh troubles and tests him at every moment. Instead of waking up to peaceful mercies, he faces continual testing that never lets up. Life is indeed a constant test of faith, but God uses trials to refine His people rather than destroy them.

Job cries out to ask how long God will keep His piercing gaze fixed upon him. He begs for just a momentary pause in his pain, using an everyday saying about having enough time to swallow his saliva. He feels utterly exhausted by the relentless pressure of his affliction.

Job addresses God as the watcher who observes all human actions. He asks what real injury a human being could possibly cause to God, and why God has made him a target for constant attack. Even though Job defended his integrity before his friends, he openly acknowledges before God that no person is completely sinless.

Job pleads with God to forgive his sins and restore His favor before it is too late. He knows his body will soon lie in the dust of death, and once he is gone from this world, God's earthly help can reach him no more. When we recognize how short life is, we should eagerly seek the Lord's mercy and pardon.
